title: Blacklash against
content:
DAILY BITE Across the U.S., a growing number of cities and police departments are reconsidering or canceling contracts with Flock Safety, whose AI-powered cameras automatically photograph vehicles, read license plates, and allow law enforcement to search vehicle movements across a large network. ￼
The technology was introduced as a relatively inexpensive crime-fighting tool, but the scale of the network has created a different concern: surveillance. Flock cameras are now used by thousands of law-enforcement agencies, creating the possibility that a vehicle’s movements can be searched far beyond the community where the data was originally collected. Concerns have intensified over data ownership, information sharing with other agencies, including immigration authorities, and cases of improper access or inaccurate vehicle flags. ￼
My takeaway is that the controversy is bigger than Flock. AI makes surveillance dramatically cheaper and easier to scale. The important question is no longer simply whether technology can help solve crimes, but who gets to watch us, how much they can know, and what limits society wants to impose.
WHY IT MATTERS Technology can move from useful tool to surveillance infrastructure almost invisibly. Once massive amounts of everyday movement are collected, the debate shifts from public safety to something more fundamental: who controls the data, and who controls the watchers?
SOURCE POLITICO — original article⁠￼

title: Pringles produces the "perfect" chips
content:
WSJ: Inside the Long, AI-Powered Quest to Perfect Pringle-Making

Siemens: Pringles stacks data to unlock innovation leaps

The project is at a Pringles factory in Poland. Kellanova worked with Siemens for roughly four years, investing about $4–5 million, to create a real-time digital twin of the Pringles dough and production process. The live system is reportedly delivering ~10% improvement in quality, 13% less waste, and >40% return on the investment; Siemens separately describes a 10% capacity increase and 7% energy-efficiency improvement from the broader digital-transformation program.

What is actually interesting about the Pringles case

It's easy to read the headline as:

AI makes perfect Pringles.

But technologically, something much more sophisticated is happening.

The fundamental manufacturing problem is raw-material variability.

Potato/flour ingredients don't arrive with exactly identical properties every day. Variables include moisture, particle size, starch/protein characteristics and other properties. Historically, experienced operators compensated through tacit knowledge: this dough looks/feels different today, so adjust the recipe or machine.

Pringles and Siemens are effectively converting that operator experience into a data/model-driven control strategy.

Conceptually:

             RAW MATERIAL
                  │
       Moisture / particle size /
       protein / ingredient variation
                  │
                  ▼
              SENSORS
                  │
                  ▼
          REAL-TIME DATA
                  │
                  ▼
        DIGITAL TWIN OF DOUGH
                  │
      Virtual representation of
      dough/process behaviour
                  │
                  ▼
             AI MODEL
                  │
     Predict dough quality / behaviour
                  │
                  ▼
       OPTIMAL PROCESS SETTINGS
                  │
      "Given today's ingredients,
       how should we run?"
                  │
                  ▼
              OPERATOR
                  │
                  ▼
          MACHINE / PROCESS
                  │
                  ▼
          CONSISTENT PRINGLE

Siemens says the network of sensors feeds variables including temperature, humidity and protein levels into an edge-based AI model, which calculates the appropriate dough recipe in real time to account for uncertainty in the raw materials.

And importantly, the AI currently recommends changes; humans still make the final decision.

title: Airbnb Wants to Own the Whole Trip
content:
Airbnb’s 2026 Summer Release shows how the company is expanding far beyond its original home-sharing business. After adding Experiences and Services last year, Airbnb is now introducing car rentals, airport pickups, grocery delivery and luggage storage, while also bringing thousands of boutique and independent hotels onto the platform. Nearly a quarter of Airbnb guests already rent a car during their stay, making car rental a natural extension of the business.

AI is another important part of the strategy. Airbnb is using AI to summarize more than one billion reviews, compare properties, improve trip planning and provide customer support. A shared itinerary and travel map are also designed to keep travelers inside Airbnb throughout their journey.

My takeaway: Airbnb is gradually evolving from a marketplace for accommodation into a travel super-app. Instead of earning from one booking, it wants to participate in more moments—and potentially more transactions—across the entire travel journey.

WHY IT MATTERS
The strategic shift is from selling a stay to owning the travel journey. If Airbnb succeeds, its existing accommodation business becomes the entry point for a much larger ecosystem of travel spending.

SOURCE
Airbnb Newsroom, May 20, 2026 — 2026 Summer Release: Now there’s even more to Airbnb

title: domino isn't making a smaller pizza
content:
Domino’s is launching an individual-sized pizza in the U.S. on August 31, targeting solo diners and customers who simply don’t want to share. The move reflects a broader shift in eating habits: 43% of U.S. food-service meals are now eaten alone, according to Circana data cited by The Wall Street Journal.

Domino’s already has evidence that this occasion can work in other markets. In Japan, its My Domino’s meal—designed around individual portions—sold more than 500,000 boxes in just over a month after launching in 2023. Domino’s later said the format was helping it compete directly with other quick-service restaurants and reach customers beyond traditional pizza occasions.

My takeaway: The interesting strategy isn’t simply making pizza smaller—it’s redefining the market. Domino’s traditional competitors may look like Pizza Hut or Papa Johns, but for a person deciding “What should I eat alone tonight?”, the real competition is burgers, sandwiches, bowls, takeaway meals and other convenient dinner options. By designing a product around the occasion rather than the category, Domino’s can expand its addressable market instead of merely fighting for share within pizza.

WHY IT MATTERS
A good growth strategy sometimes starts by asking the right competitive question. Don’t just ask, “Who sells the same product as us?” Ask, “What other choices does the customer consider when solving the same need?” That can reveal growth spaces hidden by traditional category definitions.

SOURCE
The Wall Street Journal — Domino’s Set to Release New Individual-Size Pizza; Domino’s Pizza Enterprises — FY23 Sustainability Report

title: Candy Crush: when the best innovation is not a new product
content:
Candy Crush launched in 2012, yet more than a decade later it remains one of mobile gaming’s most durable franchises. The Candy Crush franchise has surpassed 5 billion lifetime downloads and $20 billion in lifetime revenue, while King’s games still attract more than 200 million monthly players.

Part of its success came from redefining the gaming occasion. Candy Crush wasn’t only competing with other games—it captured small pockets of idle time: commuting, waiting in line, or simply having five spare minutes. It also reached consumers, including many middle-aged women, who weren’t the traditional target of the gaming industry.

But the deeper lesson is what King did after finding a blockbuster. Rather than abandoning Candy Crush in search of the next big hit, it continuously refreshed the franchise with new levels, events and features while preserving the familiarity that made people love it. Some players have remained with the game since its launch.

My takeaway: There are two powerful growth lessons here. First, define competition around the consumer occasion, not just the product category. Candy Crush competes for “What should I do with these five spare minutes?” Second, innovation doesn’t always mean inventing the next big thing. When you already own a powerful consumer asset, continually refreshing and extending the winner can create more value than constantly chasing its replacement.

WHY IT MATTERS
Great businesses can create growth both by discovering overlooked consumption occasions and by extending the lifetime value of assets they already own. The strategic question isn’t always “What should we launch next?” Sometimes it is “How much more value can we create from what consumers already love?”

SOURCE
The Times — King/Candy Crush profile; Activision Blizzard — Candy Crush franchise milestones; Microsoft Game Dev — The Art and Science of Evergreen Games: Minecraft & Candy Crush

title: Louis Vuitton × Singer: The Economics of Scarcity
content:
Louis Vuitton and Singer Vehicle Design unveiled two one-off Porsche 911 restorations at Monterey Car Week 2026. Built from classic 964-generation 911s, the cars combine Singer’s engineering and restoration craftsmanship with Louis Vuitton’s leatherwork, luggage, fashion and watchmaking heritage.

What makes the collaboration interesting is that Louis Vuitton isn’t simply putting its logo on a Porsche. It is extending its historic “Art of Travel” into an entire luxury ecosystem: car, bespoke luggage, watches and travel accessories. With only two cars created, scarcity itself becomes part of the proposition.

My takeaway: This is a great example of the economics of scarcity. Mass-market businesses often create value through scale and accessibility; luxury brands can create value through the opposite—rarity, craftsmanship and exclusivity. The cars themselves don’t need to become a meaningful revenue stream. Their strategic value is in strengthening desirability and expanding Louis Vuitton’s cultural universe without making the brand more commonplace.

WHY IT MATTERS
Growth doesn’t always mean selling more units. For luxury businesses, the challenge is growing brand value while protecting scarcity. The right collaboration can expand the ecosystem around a consumer’s lifestyle while making the core brand feel even more exclusive.

SOURCE
Car and Driver — Louis Vuitton × Singer Porsche 911 collaboration; Wallpaper* — Singer Vehicle Design and Louis Vuitton’s Porsche 911 project

title: From protecting wealth to protecting  financial independence
content:
Prenuptial agreements are becoming increasingly popular among ordinary couples, not just the super-rich. A 2026 U.S. Harris Poll found that 53% of engaged or married Gen Z and Millennials surveyed had signed a prenup.
Several social changes help explain this shift. People are marrying later, often bringing property, retirement savings, investments and debts into their relationships. Greater financial independence, rising asset values and more complex family structures are also making financial planning before marriage increasingly relevant.
A prenup is therefore being reframed from a sign of distrust into a tool for financial clarity and risk management.
My takeaway: This reflects a broader shift in how people approach marriage: building a shared life while maintaining individual financial autonomy. Love and financial independence are not necessarily contradictory. However, a fair agreement should also recognize non-financial contributions, such as sacrificing career opportunities to raise children.
WHY IT MATTERS
Changing attitudes toward marriage create opportunities for financial planning, legal services and accessible digital solutions. More fundamentally, the trend raises an important question: How can couples protect individual independence while building a fair and secure future together?
SOURCE
The Harris Poll — U.S. survey on prenuptial agreements, 2026. ￼
TAGS
Consumer Trends, Social Trends, Financial Planning, Marriage, Strategy

title: The AI Agent War: Intelligence is not enough
content:
Meta's new AI assistant, Muse, attracted strong investor interest, but Amazon reportedly blocked it from browsing and purchasing products on Amazon.com. Amazon cited concerns about unauthorized automated access, customer privacy and security. 
Axios
+2

The dispute highlights a fundamental tension in the emerging AI-agent economy. AI companies want assistants that can work across platforms, while established businesses have reasons to protect their customer relationships, proprietary data and transaction systems.

For Amazon, an external AI agent could potentially control product discovery and recommendations, leaving Amazon to fulfill orders while losing influence over the customer journey.

My takeaway: Building the smartest AI agent is not enough. Its value also depends on access to data, platforms and transactions. If every technology company builds a closed ecosystem, consumers may end up with fragmented assistants that cannot complete tasks across services.

WHY IT MATTERS

The next competitive advantage in AI may come not only from model intelligence but also from secure interoperability, trusted partnerships and control of the customer relationship. For consumer brands like PepsiCo, this raises a new question: How do we remain visible and relevant when AI agents increasingly influence what consumers buy?
